title: Words That Hold It Together
description: The short words in almost every Indonesian sentence: saying no, want and can, already and not yet, where to and from, and, but, because. They're what the grammar lessons build on.

items.english: not, no (before verbs and describing words)
items.registerNotes: Tidak goes before a verb or a describing word: tidak tahu (don't know), tidak mahal (not expensive). In everyday speech it's usually nggak.
items.pitfallNote: Not for nouns: that's bukan. Ini bukan kopi saya, not ini tidak kopi saya.

items.registerNotes: Bukan negates a thing or a person: Dia bukan guru (She's not a teacher). At the end of a sentence it asks for agreement: Enak, bukan? (Tasty, isn't it?)
Saya mau kopi (I'd like a coffee) is polite enough in a shop. Mau also means about to: Saya mau pulang (I'm going home). Ingin is the more formal want.
Before a verb: Saya bisa masak (I can cook). For a language, bisa alone is enough: Saya bisa sedikit bahasa Indonesia. Bisa? on its own asks Is that possible?, and the answer is Bisa or Tidak bisa.
Saya harus pergi (I have to go). Tidak harus means don't have to, not mustn't: for that, say jangan or tidak boleh.
Boleh saya duduk di sini? (May I sit here?) is the polite way to ask permission. The answer is Boleh (Sure) or Tidak boleh (You can't).
Sudah marks something as done: Saya sudah makan (I've eaten). Asked Sudah …?, answer Sudah or Belum, not ya or tidak. Casually udah.
items.pitfallNote: It doesn't always mean already in English: Sudah makan? is simply Have you eaten?

items.registerNotes: Belum is the hopeful no: Belum (not yet) to Sudah makan?, or Saya belum pernah ke Bali (I haven't been to Bali yet). Saying tidak there would sound like never.
Before a verb: Dia sedang makan (She's eating). In casual speech people say lagi instead: Aku lagi di jalan (I'm on my way).
items.pitfallNote: Sedang also means medium: ukuran sedang is a medium size.

items.registerNotes: Akan marks the future, mostly in careful speech and writing: Besok saya akan ke Jakarta. In conversation mau or nanti usually do the job.
Di is for where someone or something is: di rumah (at home), di Bali. Di mana? is Where?
items.pitfallNote: Di for being somewhere, ke for going there: Saya mau ke pasar, not Saya mau di pasar.

items.registerNotes: Ke is for movement towards somewhere: ke pasar (to the market), ke sana (there). Ke mana? is Where to?, and Mau ke mana? is a common greeting.
Dari for where from: Saya dari Selandia Baru (I'm from New Zealand). Dari mana? (Where from?) is asked in almost every first conversation.
Joins words and sentences, as in English: nasi dan ayam. With people you go somewhere with, it's dengan or sama: Saya pergi sama teman.
The spoken form of tetapi, which is for writing: Enak, tapi mahal (Tasty, but expensive).
The reason follows karena: Saya pulang karena capek. Friends often say soalnya instead.
So, for a result: Hujan, jadi kami di rumah. As a verb it means become, or go ahead: Jadi pergi? (Are we still going?)
Kalau hujan, kita naik taksi (If it rains, we'll take a taxi). Kalau saya… also means As for me…
Juga comes after the word it adds to: Saya juga (Me too), Saya mau teh juga (I'd like tea too).
Sangat goes before the describing word (sangat enak); sekali goes after it (enak sekali), and friends say banget (enak banget). All three mean very.
